questions.prompt: You migrated example.org to an Azure public DNS zone. Queries sent directly to its assigned Azure name servers return the new www A record. A fresh delegation trace still reaches the previous provider. Which configuration should you change to direct Internet DNS resolution to the new zone?

options.text: Set the registrar delegation to all four name servers assigned to the Azure zone.
options.explanation: The parent delegation selects authoritative servers. It must reference the four servers assigned to this zone.

options.text: Replace the www A record in the previous provider with the new address.
options.explanation: This might update that provider’s answer but keeps it authoritative; the goal is to move resolution to the Azure zone.

options.text: Lower the www A record TTL in the Azure zone.
options.explanation: TTL controls caching of that answer. It does not change the parent delegation that still selects the previous provider.

options.text: Copy the previous provider’s name servers into an NS record set named www in Azure.
options.explanation: A child-name NS set does not update example.org’s registrar delegation and would point www back to the old servers.

questions.prompt: The public zone example.org must return the IPv4 address of a Standard SKU Azure public IP resource at its apex and track the resource automatically. The resource provider and required permissions are configured. Which record set meets both requirements?

options.text: An apex CNAME targeting the public IP resource hostname.
options.explanation: A CNAME cannot coexist with the apex SOA and NS record sets.

options.text: An apex A alias targeting the public IP resource.
options.explanation: An A alias can reference a Standard public IP resource at the apex and follow its resource lifecycle.

options.text: An apex A record containing a manually copied IPv4 address.
options.explanation: It answers with IPv4, but a literal address is not linked to the public IP resource and does not track it automatically.

options.text: An apex AAAA alias targeting the public IP resource.
options.explanation: AAAA answers are IPv6. The requested answer is IPv4, which requires an A record set.

questions.prompt: A recursive resolver cached the old www A answer at 09:00 with TTL 3600 seconds. At 09:10, you change the authoritative answer and its TTL to 300 seconds. The resolver retains cached answers until expiry and receives no cache flush. At 09:20 it still returns the old address. What explains this result?

options.text: The old cached answer expired at 09:05, based on the newly configured TTL.
options.explanation: The later TTL change does not shorten the already cached answer’s original lifetime.

options.text: The old cached answer expired at 09:15, five minutes after the authoritative update.
options.explanation: The new TTL applies to newly retrieved answers, not retroactively to this cached answer.

options.text: The old cached answer remains valid until 10:00 under its original TTL.
options.explanation: Its 3600-second lifetime began at 09:00. At 09:20 the original cache entry has not expired.

options.text: The old cached answer remains valid until 10:10, one hour after the authoritative update.
options.explanation: Changing the authoritative record does not restart the lifetime of an existing recursive cache entry.
